tips.intro: Getting Over It on Pixelsprout is a climbing game where an orange cat in a flower pot drags itself up a pile of giant Scratch code blocks with a long hammer. This is a fan-made Scratch remake, not the original game. These tips cover the opening stretch of low when clicked blocks.
tips: Use slow, wide sweeps of the mouse.
Hook the hammer head over the top edge of a block before you pull. The pot only moves when the hammer head is pressing against something, so find an edge first.
Ease off the mouse when the pot lands somewhere flat. The cat keeps some momentum after you stop, so give it a moment to settle before the next move.
Watch the timer in the top right corner. It runs the whole time, so it is a fair way to measure whether a new approach is actually faster.
To lift the cat, rest the hammer head on the block under the pot and move the mouse down. In testing, that downward push raised the pot, so treat the hammer like a pole you press into the ground.
tips.conclusion: Treat each block as its own small puzzle. Hook an edge, pull a short distance, settle, then plan the next move.

extra_sections.heading: What you can see ahead
paragraphs: From the low pile, the tall upright when clicked block is visible ahead. Behind it you can see a green block with a plus sign and the edge of a purple block, and a yellow note box reading Getting Over It, Scratch Edition by Griffpatch hangs above that area.

controls.intro: The whole game is played with the mouse. The hammer head follows your cursor around the cat, and every move you make comes from where you plant it and which way you pull. This version is a fan-made Scratch remake by griffpatch, not the original game by Bennett Foddy.
controls.desktop: Move the mouse to swing the hammer around the cat. Press the hammer head against a block and pull the cursor the opposite way to push the pot up or along. No clicking is needed once a run starts. In an earlier session, arrow keys and WASD did nothing.
controls.mobile: This version has no on-screen Mobile Controls toggle. Touch controls were not tested, so how it plays on a touch screen is unconfirmed.
tips: On the start screen, choose New Game to begin. Sound Effects and Commentary can be switched from the same menu.
Small, steady mouse movements give the most control. Fast flicks tend to tip the pot over.
The timer in the top right starts when the run starts, so you can watch the menu for as long as you like first.
Use the full screen button in the top right corner for more room to move the mouse.

beginner-guide.intro: New to this version of Getting Over It? Here is what is on screen, what you are trying to do and how the first minute of a run usually goes.
beginner-guide.what_it_is: Getting Over It is a slow, physics-based climbing game. You control the Scratch cat, sitting in a brown flower pot, through a long hammer that follows your mouse. This Pixelsprout version is a fan-made Scratch remake: its start screen reads Getting Over It, Scratch edition with Griffpatch, and everything you climb is made of oversized Scratch code blocks, such as yellow when clicked blocks with green flags. The goal is to climb as high as you can, with blue water waiting below the blocks.
first_steps: Wait for the game to load, accept the notice if one appears, then press New Game. A quick click may not start it, so hold the click until the timer appears.
Before you climb, move the mouse in a slow circle and watch how the hammer swings around the pot.
Hook the hammer head on the nearest yellow block and pull back to drag the cat onto it.
Work across the low pile of when clicked blocks. There are gaps between some blocks, and you can pass over a gap without falling.
beginner-guide.who_its_for: Players who enjoy a stubborn precision challenge and can laugh off losing progress, and anyone who knows Scratch and wants to see its code blocks used as climbing terrain.

extra_sections.heading: What the start screen shows
paragraphs: The menu shows the title, the line Scratch edition with Griffpatch, a New Game option and toggles for Sound Effects and Commentary. A World Record time appears in the top right.
Once you press New Game, the menu goes away and a run timer takes the place of the record time in the corner.

similar.intro: Getting Over It is about one awkward control scheme and a lot of patience. Every move happens through a hammer, progress is slow and a single slip can throw away a minute of climbing. If you liked that mix of physics, careful mouse control and starting over without much fuss, try more games from the Pixelsprout catalog next. When you pick one, look for games where the challenge comes from controlling your own movement rather than from enemies or timers. This version is a fan-made Scratch remake by griffpatch, not the original game by Bennett Foddy.

faqs.question: Is this the original Getting Over It?
faqs.answer: No. It is a fan-made Scratch recreation by griffpatch, not the original game by Bennett Foddy. The start screen credits it as a Scratch edition with Griffpatch, and the levels are built from giant Scratch code blocks.

faqs.question: How do you move in Getting Over It?
faqs.answer: You only control the hammer. Move the mouse so the hammer head presses against a block, then pull the cursor the other way to push the cat and its pot.

faqs.question: Do the arrow keys or WASD do anything?
faqs.answer: No. Arrow keys and WASD had no effect when they were tried in an earlier session. The game is played with the mouse alone.

faqs.question: What is the start of the climb like?
faqs.answer: It begins on a low pile of when clicked blocks with gaps between some of them. In a replay, the cat crossed a gap without falling, and the tall upright when clicked block was visible ahead.

faqs.question: Can you turn off the commentary?
faqs.answer: Yes. The start screen has separate Sound Effects and Commentary toggles next to the New Game option.

faqs.question: What do the timer and World Record show?
faqs.answer: A timer in the top right corner counts up during a run. The start screen shows a World Record time in the same spot.
